WHEN Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, purchased Canterville Chase, everybody assured him that he was acting very foolishly, since there could be no question that the house was haunted. Indeed, Lord Canterville himself, a gentleman of the most scrupulous honour, had thought it incumbent upon him to tell Mr. Otis so when they began discussing the terms.

‘We have had no wish to inhabit the place ourselves,’ Lord Canterville said, ‘since my grandaunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, was terrified into a fit from which she never entirely recovered, when two skeleton hands were laid upon her shoulders while she dressed for dinner. And I am obliged to inform you, Mr. Otis, that several surviving members of my family have seen the ghost, as has our parish rector, the Rev. Augustus Dampier, a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. Following the Duchess’s unfortunate accident, not one of our younger servants would remain with us, and Lady Canterville frequently slept very little at night because of the inexplicable sounds proceeding from the corridor and the library.’

‘My Lord,’ replied the Minister, ‘I shall take the furniture and the ghost at their assessed value. Mine is a modern country, where we possess everything money will purchase; and with all our lively young fellows painting the Old World red and taking away your finest actresses and prima-donnas, I calculate that, if Europe had anything like a ghost, we should soon have it back home in a public museum, or travelling about as an exhibition.’

‘I am afraid the ghost does exist,’ Lord Canterville said with a smile, ‘although it may have declined the advances of your enterprising impresarios. People have known it well for three centuries—since 1584, indeed—and it invariably appears before any member of our family dies.’

‘Well, the family physician does that too, Lord Canterville. But a ghost is no such thing as exists, sir, and I reckon Nature’s laws will hardly be set aside for the British aristocracy.’

‘Certainly you are very natural in America,’ replied Lord Canterville, who had not altogether understood Mr. Otis’s final remark, ‘and provided you have no objection to a ghost in the house, all is well. You must only recollect that I gave you warning.’

Some weeks later the purchase was concluded, and when the season ended the Minister took his family down to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis, who as Miss Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street had been a renowned New York belle, was now an exceedingly handsome woman of middle age, possessing fine eyes and a magnificent profile.

A time arrives in the life of every properly constituted boy when he longs furiously to go off somewhere and dig up buried treasure. One day this longing seized Tom without warning. He went forth in search of Joe Harper, but could not find him. Then he tried Ben Rogers, who had gone fishing. Before long he chanced upon Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would serve. Tom led him to a secluded spot and confided the business to him. Huck agreed. Huck was always ready to join any undertaking that promised amusement and called for no capital, for he possessed an inconvenient excess of the kind of time that is not money. ‘Where shall we dig?’ Huck asked.

‘Oh, pretty near anywhere.’

‘What, is it hidden everywhere?’

‘No, it certainly ain’t. They hide it in mighty special places, Huck—on islands sometimes, or in rotten chests underneath the tip of a branch on an old dead tree, right where its shadow falls at midnight. But mostly it’s beneath the floors of ha’nted houses.’

‘Who puts it there?’

‘Robbers, naturally—who did you suppose? Sunday-school sup’rintendents?’

‘I dunno. If it belonged to me I wouldn’t bury it; I’d spend it enjoying myself.’

‘I would too. Only robbers don’t act that way. They always hide it away and let it stay.’

‘Don’t they ever fetch it again?’

‘No. They mean to, but mostly they forget the landmarks, or they die instead. Anyhow, it stays there for ages getting rusty, till somebody comes across an old yellow paper explaining how to find the marks. You have to puzzle over that paper for about a week, because nearly all of it’s signs and hy’roglyphics.’

‘Hyro—what?’

‘Hy’roglyphics—pictures and such, you know, that look like they don’t signify anything.’

‘You got one of those papers, Tom?’

‘No.’

‘Then how’ll you find those marks?’

‘I don’t need marks. They always bury treasure beneath a ha’nted house, or on an island, or under a dead tree with one branch sticking out. We’ve tried Jackson’s Island a bit already, and we can try again another time. And there’s that old ha’nted house up the Still-House branch, besides plenty of dead-limb trees—dead loads of them.’

‘Is there some under every one?’

‘What a thing to say! No!’

‘Then how’ll you tell which to try?’

‘Try every one of ’em!’

‘Why, Tom, that’ll take the whole summer.’

‘Well, what difference does that make? Say you find a brass pot holding a hundred dollars, all gray and rusty, or a rotten chest packed with di’monds. What about that?’

Huck’s eyes shone.

‘That’s bully. Plenty good enough for me. Give me those hundred dollars, and I won’t ask for any di’monds.’

But he had oppressed no one and sent no one to prison. Far from forcing people harshly to pay what they owed him, he had freely given up his claims. He had gone out into a world that offered him no favours, made a place for himself, and earned his own living. Monsieur Gabelle had managed the poor, debt-ridden estate under written orders to spare the people and give them whatever little help was possible: in winter, whatever fuel the demanding creditors would allow; in summer, whatever produce could be kept from their grasp. Surely, to protect himself, Gabelle had offered these instructions as evidence in his defence. They must therefore come to light now.

This strengthened the desperate decision Charles Darnay had begun to reach: he would go to Paris.

Yes. Like the sailor in the old tale, winds and currents had carried him within reach of the magnetic Loadstone Rock. It was pulling him towards it, and he had to go. Every thought that entered his mind drove him faster and more steadily towards that terrible attraction. Beneath everything lay an uneasiness: evil people were pursuing evil purposes in his own unhappy country, while he, who could hardly doubt that he was better than they were, remained elsewhere. He was doing nothing there to stop the killing or to speak up for mercy and humanity. He had partly suppressed this feeling, though it still partly reproached him. Then he had been forced into a direct comparison with the brave old gentleman whose sense of duty was so strong. That comparison put him in a poor light. Immediately afterwards had come Monseigneur’s sneers, which wounded him deeply, and Stryver’s, especially crude and irritating because of old grievances. After those had come Gabelle’s letter: an innocent prisoner, facing death, had appealed to his justice, his honour, and his good name.

He had made his decision. He must go to Paris.

Yes. The Loadstone Rock was drawing him closer, and he must sail on until he struck it. He knew nothing of any rock; he could scarcely see danger at all. He looked at his past actions through the intentions behind them, even though he had left his work unfinished. He believed France would gratefully recognise those intentions once he appeared there to explain them. Then he was filled with that glorious dream of doing good, the hopeful illusion that so often deceives well-meaning people. In that dream he even imagined himself possessing some power to direct the furious Revolution, now running so terribly out of control.
